problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =\sqrt{3}\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$

examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Complex Eigenvector of a Matrix Given a Complex Eigenvalue
examples.problem:
Find an eigenvector of 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/7dad070080562e459c926f5c8fa3d71a56981d68bd3ed4aae768c2f7450685a3.png)
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-3+4\textrm{i}.$
examples.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-3+4\textrm{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-3+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -3+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4\text{i} & 4 \\ -4 & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-4\text{i}{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}-4\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-3+4\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
x_1 = -\textrm{i}x_2.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/6786c7bc4d12bc3ee1a335eeb45967475850a585ec36805fe81aa76360d5a729.png)

Setting $x_2=1,$ we get the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041802/assets/a73682dbe1dfccc14e5b3f0c68aa6e6aa7eb7a67bb475efbbaeaa1e886585554.png)

feedback.problem:
Determine if $v=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].$
If so, then what is the corresponding eigenvalue?
feedback.worked_solution:
The eigenvectors are non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-\text{i} \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{\text{i}}^{2}-\text{i} \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\text{i}(\text{i}+1) \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =(1+\text{i})[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =(1+\text{i})v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=(1+\text{i})v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =1+\text{i}.$
